newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Crop institute boosts Nigerian cassava output.
newsitem.headline: Crop institute boosts Nigerian cassava output.

text.p: High-yielding and disease-resistant varieties of cassava developed by a research institute have helped to boost production of the crop in Nigeria, officials and scientists said.

"We have been conducting research on cassava for nearly three decades and we're happy the varieties we bred and which are now used by farmers have shored up Nigerian production," Mpoki Bokanga, senior crop researcher at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), told Reuters in the southwestern city of Ibadan.
IITA, founded in 1967 to improve crop yields in Africa, has its headquarters in Ibadan and several other substations on the continent. It is funded by donations from the World Bank and U.N. agencies.

Cassava, a root tuber similar to yam and grown on the marginal soils of lowland farms in Nigeria's rain forest and the middle belt states, is a staple food in most homes of Africa's most populous nation of 100 million.
Bokanga said IITA cassava was highly resistant to the African cassava mosaic and bacterial blight, two diseases that almost wiped the crop out of Nigeria between 1970 and 1980.
"Since 1991, Nigeria has become the largest producer of cassava in the world," Bokanga said.

Olumide Tewe, a crop scientist at the nearby University of Ibadan, who has worked on some projects with IITA, said, "Through a continent-wide biological programme, IITA has brought under control the cassava mealybug, a devastating pest imported from Latin America, which once threatened the crop in Africa."
IITA spokesman Taye Babaleye said in addition to boosting Nigeria's production, the institute had tried to prove cassava was a commercial crop.
"It's a cash crop for farmers and fast turning into an important industrial raw material," he added.
Agriculture ministry officials said Nigeria produced 31.4 million tonnes of cassava in 1995.
Given the country's increasing production, the government wanted to diversify the economy via export of the crop after local demand had been met, they said.
